title: Partition of parallel energy transport in the TCV divertor
abstract: Power sharing between conductive and convective transport and ions and electrons plays a central role in determining divertor performance in magnetically confined fusion plasmas. Direct measurements of the individual contributions to the parallel energy flux remain scarce due to the difficulty of simultaneously measuring ion temperature, electron temperature, plasma density, and plasma flow velocity with sufficient spatial resolution. Herein, a combination of diagnostics and SOLPS-ITER simulations is used to study the parallel energy flux in the outer divertor leg of the TCV tokamak. Dedicated Ohmic L-mode experiments were performed in both magnetic field directions, in attached and partially detached divertor conditions. Local measurements of ion temperature and parallel flow velocity were obtained using the Tangential Divertor Spectroscopy System (TDSS) and a spatial inversion technique, with electron temperature and density measured by Thomson scattering. Together, these measurements have, for the first time on TCV, provided a direct decomposition of the parallel energy flux into ion and electron, conductive and convective contributions. Magnetic field reversal revealed a strong influence of E × B drifts on the parallel flow structure, resulting in a shift of the ion convective energy flux profile. A thermal decoupling between ions and electrons in the scrape-off layer was observed, with T i ≲ T e near the separatrix and T i > T e in the far SOL. The reconstructed energy fluxes indicate that electron conduction dominates power transport near the separatrix in attached, low-density conditions. As the density is increased towards detachment, conductive transport decreases, and convection becomes the dominant transport channel, carrying up to 60%–80% of the total parallel energy flux. SOLPS-ITER simulations including magnetic drifts reproduced the measured upstream and divertor plasma conditions, the magnetic-field-direction dependence of the flow profiles, and the observed energy transport partitioning between ions and electrons. These simulations further indicate that cross-field E × B convection substantially redistributes the poloidal energy flux to the divertor target. Ion-driven energy transport constitutes a substantial fraction of the divertor power exhaust that requires accurate characterisation to model and predict heat loads.

title: Life-Cycle Flow-Induced Vibration Characteristics of Nuclear Fuel Rods Subject to Multi-Source Uncertainties
abstract: Flow-induced vibration (FIV) affects grid-to-rod fretting wear and the service life of nuclear fuel rods. During operation, irradiation and corrosion alter material properties and spacer-grid supports, while axial coolant turbulence and local transverse disturbances generate stochastic excitation. Their combined effects on life-cycle nonlinear vibration and correlated uncertainties remain insufficiently quantified. This study develops a multi-span beam model incorporating axial and transverse flow excitation, burnup-dependent preload relaxation, grid-to-rod clearance, and unilateral contact. Stochastic time-domain integration is employed to predict the vibration response, while a non-probabilistic ellipsoidal model quantifies response bounds and parameter correlations. Including transverse-flow excitation increases the predicted root-mean-square (RMS) displacement by 19% at 3 m/s and reduces the experimental prediction error by 20.1%. The maximum RMS displacement increases from 4.92 μm at the beginning of life to 14.00 μm near 34.3 GW d/t, before decreasing to 9.11 μm at 50 GW d/t. The response bounds evolve non-monotonically, while positive correlation between transverse-flow parameters widens the uncertainty interval.

title: False Data Injection Detection in Nuclear Power Plants using Autoencoder with Latent-Conditioned Mahalanobis Scoring
abstract: As instrumentation and control (I&C) systems in nuclear power plants (NPPs) are digitalized, cybersecurity concerns have grown. A particular concern is false data injection (FDI) attacks, which can induce malfunctions of plant systems and degrade the situational awareness of main control room operators. Against such attacks, monitoring the integrity of process data can serve as a defensive barrier, and autoencoders have been studied as a promising tool for this purpose. However, their reconstruction error varies across operating conditions even for normal data, which forces the detection threshold above the errors of rare but normal conditions and allows well-crafted manipulations to evade detection. To improve sensitivity where false alarms must be minimized, this study proposes latent-conditioned Mahalanobis scoring, which requires no modification of the conventional autoencoder. The method clusters the latent vectors of calibration data, estimates the mean and covariance of reconstruction residuals per cluster, and scores a query input by the Mahalanobis distance under its nearest clusters' statistics. Experiments with emergency operation data from an NPP simulator and 10 synthetic FDI scenarios injected during accident conditions show that the proposed score outperforms the conventional reconstruction-error score and other scoring methods at high specificity levels.

title: Development of Collapse Pressure Prediction Equations for Helical-Coil Steam Generator Tubes in Small Modular Reactors Considering Geometric Effects
abstract: Small modular reactors (SMR) use helical-coil steam generator (HCSG) tubes for efficient heat transfer in compact spaces. Their collapse under external pressure depends on pitch angle, diameter-to-thickness ratio ( D / t ), coil diameter, and initial ovality, which existing straight-tube prediction equations do not clearly account for. Thus, this study developed geometry-based correlations from parametric finite element (FE) analyses using the RIKS arc-length method. The analyses covered D/t = 6.8–11.3, pitch angles of 1–30°, initial ovalities of 0–4%, and coil diameters of 500–6000 mm. Collapse pressure decreases substantially with increasing pitch angle, whereas the coil-diameter effect is secondary over the tested range, identifying pitch angle as the dominant helix-related parameter. The proposed correlation reproduces the FE results with a mean absolute percentage error of 3.33% and a root-mean-square error of 1.90 MPa. The correlation should be interpreted as a preliminary interpolation for homogeneous elastic-perfectly plastic (EPP) tubes within the calibrated ranges. At the combined extreme of D / t = 11.3, α = 30°, and δ = 4%, it overpredicted the FE collapse pressure by 19.8%; case-specific FE analysis is therefore recommended for extreme geometries. The correlation is not a substitute for ASME Section III assessment or alloy- and temperature-specific nonlinear evaluation.

title: Assessing Saudi Arabia’s readiness for fusion RDI: A comparative framework and roadmap to 2035
abstract: This study develops and applies a six-dimensional Fusion RDI Readiness Framework to assess Saudi Arabia’s preparedness for participation in fusion research, development, and innovation (RDI) and to examine possible pathways toward 2035. The framework is grounded in National Innovation Systems, the IAEA Milestones Approach, Technology and Manufacturing Readiness Levels, and fusion-specific roadmaps and national strategies. It assesses readiness across governance and vision, regulatory and safety capability, research infrastructure and capability, human capital and education, industry and innovation ecosystem, and international cooperation and collaboration. The framework is first applied comparatively to the Republic of Korea, Japan, the United States, the United Kingdom, China, and Russia, with the European fusion ecosystem considered separately as a supranational reference. The comparison shows that national fusion capability develops through different combinations of domestic infrastructure, international participation, regulation, workforce development, and industrial involvement, rather than through a single model. Application to Saudi Arabia identifies a significant base of transferable capabilities in nuclear regulation, university education, research infrastructure, RDI mechanisms, industrial capacity, and international nuclear cooperation, while also identifying important fusion-specific gaps. Three strategic pathways are therefore considered: Baseline/No Dedicated Fusion Engagement, Partnership-Led Engagement, and Focused National Capability Development. Rather than identifying a predetermined preferred pathway, the study proposes a conditional roadmap for 2026–2035 in which deeper domestic investment depends on documented research activity, specialist capability, partnership outcomes, and industrial participation. The framework provides a structured basis for evaluating national fusion RDI readiness and supporting evidence-based decisions on future engagement.

title: Between hype and uncertainty: Expert assessments of nuclear small-modular reactors (SMRs) under data center energy boom
abstract: The unprecedented growth in artificial intelligence and data center energy demand has renewed interest in small modular reactors (SMRs) as a potential low-carbon baseload solution. Yet significant uncertainty persists around the techno-economic characteristics and policy solutions necessary for SMR commercialization in the United States. This inadvertently leaves policymakers navigating critical decisions about resource allocation, regulatory reform, and long-term energy planning without a clear picture of near-term prospects of SMRs. This study addresses that gap by conducting a mixed methods expert survey of 33 professionals from industry, academia, government, utilities, and think tanks. Results collectively suggest a moderate confidence in an outlook with high overnight capital cost of over $6000/kW and cost overruns of over 30%, falling short of DOE's commercialization target. They also reflect cautious optimism rooted in the expectation of an incremental learning rate due to rapid electricity demand growth from data centers and standardization of design. Overall, experts highlight a significant gap between promotional narratives and realistic techno-economic trajectories.

title: Stellarator Plasma Start-up Model Based on Energy Confinement Time Scaling Laws, Experimental Verification and Numerical Simulation Results
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Based on the energy confinement time scaling law of stellarator in the low-confinement mode, combined with energy balance equation and the plasma propagation and power deposition equations of the electron cyclotron wave in the three-dimensional magnetic field, a stellarator plasma start-up model including electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH) and impurity radiation power loss is established. Validation against W7-X experimental data demonstrates good agreement in the temporal evolution of electron temperature and radiation losses, which verified that the model can correctly give the plasma start-up results of the stellarator under ECRH. This model is applied to predict the results of plasma start-up under 28 GHz ECRH for China Helical Device 1 (CN-H1) stellarator. The effects of the initial electron-to-ion temperature ratio (Te/Ti), ECRH injection power (Pinj), deposition position and effective charge number Z_{\text{eff}} on start-up are systematically studied and analyzed. The results show that the initial Te/Ti ratio affects only the ramp-up rate, while the final steady-state electron and ion temperature remain unaffected. Higher Pinj accelerates electron temperature rise and increases flat-top electron temperature, whereas the ion temperature exhibits the opposite trend, decreasing with increasing Pinj. The deposition location has a decisive impact on the start-up outcome: only core deposition on the low-field side leads to a successful start-up, while high-field side and off-axis low-field side depositions fail owing to refractive deviation of the ray trajectory and insufficient absorption, respectively. The steady-state electron and ion temperatures are insensitive to {\mathrm{Z}}_{\text{eff}} within a reasonable range.</jats:p>

title: Investigation of Hydrodynamic Parameters for FAC-Induced Wall Thinning in Elbow Pipes Using CFD and Machine Learning
abstract: Flow-accelerated corrosion (FAC) is a major degradation mechanism in piping systems and is significant in fittings such as elbows, where local hydrodynamic conditions vary substantially. In this study, the relationship between hydrodynamic parameters and FAC-induced wall thinning was investigated through a combination of experimental measurements, computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations, and machine learning techniques. Accelerated FAC tests were conducted to obtain wall-thinning data over a wide range of locations, including the elbow and the upstream and downstream straight sections. CFD simulations were performed to extract velocity and vorticity components in the axial, circumferential, and radial directions. Surface morphology analysis using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) revealed that the size and density of scallop patterns were closely associated with the axial and circumferential velocity components, indicating that local flow characteristics strongly influence FAC-induced wall thinning. An artificial neural network (ANN) model was developed using CFD-derived hydrodynamic parameters as inputs and experimentally measured wall-thinning data as outputs. The results demonstrated that velocity and vorticity components are effective predictors of wall thinning. Furthermore, ANN-based geometry factors agreed with measurements and were below CHECWORKS predictions. Applicability is limited to the tested elbow and operating condition (7 m/s, 150 °C, pH 7); extension requires further data.

title: Reactor operation induced thermal effects on neutron flux measurements using 3He neutron detectors at a TRIGA Mk II research reactor
abstract: A variation of the measured neutron flux using 3 He detectors at a TRIGA Mk II nuclear research reactor during steady-state operation is reported in this article. The observed effect shows a statistically significant anti-correlation ( > 7 σ ) between the temperature in the reactor pool and recorded neutron count rates. Following reactor start-up under nominal operating conditions, the effect occurs for a specific time period until both thermal equilibrium and a constant neutron count rate are reached. Simultaneous neutron and temperature measurements are performed in different configurations around the reactor in order to gain qualitative insights about the temperature dependent count rate behavior.

title: In-situ repair of eroded tungsten plasma facing components using wire arc directed energy deposition
abstract: Within existing conceptual studies, it is assumed a fusion reactor will require replacement of its divertor every 2 years and the blanket module every 5 to 6 years. The complexity of this replacement operation requires advanced remote-handling technologies and generates a large rad-waste stream. Keeping these challenges in mind, the in-situ repair of plasma-facing components has been proposed to extend their working life and reduce required reactor downtime. This work explores the application of wire arc deposition to in-situ repair of tungsten PFCs with both gas tungsten arc welding and plasma arc welding systems. Additive manufacturing technologies have been previously explored to allow for in-situ repair, but many of these technologies cannot be adapted to the requirements of the reactor environment. We develop a methodology that allows for the crack-free deposition of pure tungsten onto tungsten substrates by preheating the substrates with the welding torch. This methodology is then extended to filling simulated erosions in the tungsten substrate, and a surface correction process is developed to ensure a uniform surface finish on repaired tiles. A comparison between pure tungsten and tungsten-rhenium alloy substrates was conducted to evaluate their relative compatibility with the wire arc repair process. Extensive material characterization was also performed on the deposited tungsten material to establish its properties relative to the manufactured substrate. Collectively, these results form the foundation to develop a robust PFC repair methodology using wire arc deposition.

title: Optimizing entrained-flow reactors for biomass gasification: a novel framework for controlling slag–refractory interactions and enhancing durability
abstract: Biomass-fed entrained-flow reactors are promising for syngas production, but slag formation and refractory degradation remain major challenges for their reliable operation. This study investigates the coupled effects of biomass ash chemistry, slag phase evolution, heat transfer, and slag–refractory interactions, with particular emphasis on the cold-crucible concept. Thermodynamic modelling and laboratory-scale experiments were combined to characterize inorganic species transformation, slag liquidus temperature, and the interaction of miscanthus-derived slag with silicon carbide (SiC) refractory. Alkali- and chlorine-containing species were found to play a major role in deposit formation, with KCl identified as a potentially corrosive species. The experimentally determined liquidus temperature of miscanthus ash was approximately 1230 °C, compared with 1324 °C predicted by thermodynamic calculations, highlighting limitations in existing databases for alkali-rich systems. At 1300 °C, molten slag caused limited SiC infiltration and dissolution, with penetration restricted to approximately 100 µm. Under a controlled thermal gradient, a stable 8 mm solid slag layer developed, providing thermal protection to the refractory. The liquid slag/solid slag and solid slag/SiC interfaces stabilized at 1231 °C and 1130 °C, respectively, corresponding to a heat flux of 12.9 kW m −2 . These results support the potential of cooled SiC linings and self-forming slag layers for improving wall stability and provide a basis for optimizing reactor operating conditions.

title: First assessment of neutral gas transport in the EU DEMO low aspect ratio divertor
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Efficient removal of neutral particles from the divertor region is essential for maintaining acceptable plasma conditions and ensuring reliable operation of future fusion reactors. In the present work, the neutral gas dynamics in the sub-divertor region of the DEMO low aspect ratio (LAR) divertor are investigated using three-dimensional Direct Simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) simulations. A 3D complex model of one divertor sector is employed to quantify particle exhaust through the pumping openings, neutral leakage through the toroidal and poloidal gaps, and the corresponding pressure and temperature distributions. The influence of the divertor entrance pressure and the effective pumping probability is systematically examined, together with the effect of asymmetric pressure conditions at the divertor entry gaps. The results show that the pumping probability is the dominant parameter controlling the exhaust performance, increasing the pumped particle flux while reducing neutral leakage, particularly through the toroidal gaps. Changes in the divertor entrance pressure mainly affect the absolute pressure levels, with only a limited influence on the overall flow field. Simulations with asymmetric injection pressures indicate that pressure imbalances between the two divertor entry gaps have moderate effect on the neutral transport. Over the investigated conditions, 57.9%–86.4% of the incoming neutral particles return to the plasma region through the divertor entry gaps, while the pumped fraction ranges from 1.74% to 22% of the incoming flux, increasing with both the pumping probability and the injection pressure. To complement the DSMC analysis, a reduced-order conductance model is developed for rapid engineering assessments. The model captures the overall pressure distribution and DSMC trends with an average absolute deviation of ∼29% in only a few seconds, making it suitable for preliminary design studies. Overall, these results quantify neutral gas transport and pumping performance in the DEMO LAR divertor and support particle exhaust development.</jats:p>

title: Development of one-dimensional plasma transport code and the application to MPS-LD linear plasma device
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>To investigate plasma transport in the Multiple Plasma Simulation Linear Device (MPS-LD), a one-dimensional (1D) finite-volume (FV) fluid code LDPFT1D for edge plasma transport along the magnetic field is developed and coupled with a Monte Carlo (MC) code MCNT for neutral-particle transport. The coupled code LDPFT-MCNT1D is highly modular and extensible, allowing it to be flexibly adapted to various physical problems. LDPFT1D is benchmarked against the BOUT++ LPD module, and LDPFT-MCNT 1D is compared against experimental measurements from hydrogen plasma discharges in MPS-LD. Overall agreement is obtained in both comparisons, supporting the numerical implementation and physical model. Using LDPFT-MCNT 1D, the effects of H⁻ mediated dissociative attachment molecular activated recombination (DA-MAR) on plasma transport are investigated. The results show that DA-MAR provides an additional H⁺ loss channel in the near target region through dissociative attachment and mutual neutralization. The resulting reduction in the local net particle source decreases the electron density, ion flux, and heat flux at the target. Within the parameter range considered in this study, the contribution of DA-MAR to the total volumetric loss of H⁺ exhibits a pronounced dependence on the electron temperature. DA-MAR is primarily active in the low-temperature range 2 eV < Te < 4.5 eV, where it accounts for approximately 20%–30% of the total volumetric loss of H⁺. These results demonstrate that DA-MAR is an important molecular process affecting hydrogen plasma transport.</jats:p>

title: A Feasibility Study of a Molten Salt Fast Reactor with Moderated Blanket for Long-Lived Fission Product Transmutation
abstract: A conceptual design study has been performed for a 300–megawatt thermal (MWt) fast spectrum molten chloride salt reactor coupled with an external moderated blanket for transmutation of long-lived fission products (LLFPs) Tc-99, I-129, and Se-79, which supplies electricity to a proton accelerator of the spallation neutron transmuter for transmutation of other LLFPs of Zr-93, Sn-126, and Cs-135. The design involves a cylindrical flowing fuel core and an external D2O-moderated target blanket in which LLFPs are loaded in elemental forms with no isotopic separation as technetium metal pins, cladded selenium pins, and MgI2 diluted in the heavy water. Design parameters were determined via a series of parametric studies including LLFP loading pattern optimization, addition of a technetium thermal neutron filter, enrichment of the chloride salt with Cl-37, and increase in core height-to-diameter ratio to increase radial neutron leakage to the blanket. Several reactor design metrics, such as reactivity feedback coefficients, reactor shutdown margin, precursor drift effect, and material thermal margins, were analyzed to ensure satisfaction of design constraints. The resulting net transmutation rates are 31.55 kg/yr of Tc-99, 12.28 kg/yr of I-129, and 0.77 kg/yr of Se-79. Other LLFPs that experience net production in the fuel salt will be treated with the spallation neutron transmuter to fully transmute the priority LLFPs. The proposed 300-MWt molten salt reactor (MSR) transmuter can effectively transmute the Tc-99, Se-79, and I-129 LLFPs from a 3500-MWt pressurized water reactor and produces energy for driving complementary transmutation technologies.

title: EMC3-EIRENE predictions of edge plasma parameters in the standard configuration of Wendelstein 7-X equipped with a tungsten-based island divertor
abstract: In 2021, a new divertor design project has been launched for the stellarator experiment Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) to prepare the replacement of the current water-cooled carbon-based island divertor with a tungsten-based divertor for future experimental exploitation (2030s). As a first theoretical approach to investigate the potential divertor conditions in the standard configuration of W7-X with a tungsten-based divertor in the current design, EMC3-EIRENE, the standard modeling tool for boundary plasmas in non-axisymmetric 3D magnetic configurations, is used in predictive manner. Material-dependent changes in the neutral particle density in the divertor plasma are related to differences in particle and energy reflectivity of carbon (C) and tungsten (W). A scan in separatrix density and heating power flux into the scrape-off layer in a hydrogen plasma predicts that plasma detachment with sufficiently low target electron temperatures to suppress W sputtering is not achievable without impurity seeding and steady-state heat-fluxes exceed the thermal load limit of 10 MW m − 2 at elevated heating powers and low plasma density. Introducing neon (Ne) as recycling impurity species efficiently reduces the divertor plasma temperature in the simulation by strong power dissipation via impurity radiation. However, penetration of Ne into the confined region suggests limitations for achievable plasma densities. Operation at high heating power allows to concentrate the Ne radiation in the edge plasma to achieve high temperature gradients in the divertor. Estimation of W gross erosion by highly ionized Ne emphasizes the need to operate in detached conditions to reduce significantly the W source at the divertor targets and baffles.

title: Genuine Multi-Objective Optimization of Multi-Step Square Cascades for 82Kr Isotope Separation: A Comparative Study of Metaheuristic Algorithms
abstract: This study formulates multi-step square cascade design for 82 Kr enrichment as a genuine multi-objective optimization problem, simultaneously maximizing total recovery and final product purity-two conflicting objectives-while treating the entire S-step process as an integrated coupled system in which operating parameters of all steps are adjusted simultaneously. Four algorithms-Non-dominated Sorting Genetic Algorithm-II (NSGA-II), Pareto Envelope-based Selection Algorithm-II (PESA-II), Multi-Objective Grey Wolf Optimizer (MOGWO), and Non-dominated Sorting Gravitational Search Algorithm (NSGSA)-are compared across three test cases (N = 48, S = 6; N = 26, S = 8; and a 2.5 SCCM minimum flow constraint). Assessment using Hypervolume (HV), Spacing (SP), Spread (Δ), and Mean Ideal Distance (MID), supported by pairwise Mann–Whitney U tests with Holm correction, reveals no single dominant algorithm; notably, in HV, MOGWO differs significantly from NSGA-II in all cases. The trade-off shows that achieving 95% final purity reduces recovery by approximately 41.9% compared to 50% purity targets. The minimum flow constraint imposes an inherent physical efficiency penalty, estimated at approximately 32.6% via a single-objective optimization at ∼ 95% purity, while larger reductions in multi-objective runs (up to 93%) reflect algorithmic difficulty in navigating the constrained feasible region. The Pareto fronts provide explicit decision-support maps.

title: Design and Field Validation of a Novel Split-Cylindrical Tungsten Collimator for Improving Spatial Resolution in CANDU Spent Fuel Verification
abstract: The Optical Fiber Probe System (OFPS), used by the IAEA to verify CANDU spent fuel, often fails to resolve signals from closely stacked fuel bundles because radiation from adjacent bundles overlaps at the detector. The Improved Optical fiber-based VErification System (IOVES) adopted a high-light-output scintillator and improved detection performance, but could not resolve masked peaks, as this limitation stems from the measurement geometry rather than detector sensitivity. To overcome this geometric limitation, a micro-scale, split-cylindrical tungsten collimator was designed to fit within the narrow 17.65 mm gap between fuel bundle columns; its central window admits lateral radiation from the target bundle while shielding diagonal and axial interference from adjacent layers. MCNP simulations showed that a collimator with a 2 mm window improved the Peak-to-Valley Ratio (PVR) by approximately 18% over the uncollimated probe. Field tests were then conducted at Wolsong Unit 3. The collimator-equipped probe reduced interference between adjacent bundles and improved the PVR in all evaluated layers, increasing the average PVR by 5.6% and 9.3% in the two fuel columns. By enhancing overall bundle discrimination, the proposed collimator is expected to help reduce secondary visual verifications and improve the efficiency and reliability of safeguards inspections.

title: A non-perturbative framework for ion stopping in partially ionized warm dense matter with a physics-informed neural-network solver
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ion energy deposition in dense plasmas is of central importance to ion-beam-driven inertial confinement fusion and high-energy-density physics. In the Bragg-peak regime, the stopping power governs the spatial distribution of deposited energy and therefore strongly affects the formation of warm dense states and the efficiency of ion fast ignition. In this regime, the projectile velocity becomes comparable to the characteristic velocity of target electrons, and the beam–plasma interaction may enter a nonlinear, non-perturbative scattering regime in which Born-based perturbative treatments are no longer adequate. For partially ionized warm dense matter, additional complexity arises from charge-state distributions, bound-electron response and dynamic screening. Here, we develop a physically constrained, self-consistent non-perturbative framework for ion stopping in warm dense matter. The approach combines formal quantum-scattering relations, a charge-state-resolved collisional–radiative model and multiscale effective interaction potentials. In the strong-scattering regime, non-perturbative phase shifts are obtained from the Calogero equation using a variable-phase physics-informed neural-network solver, while the Born limit is recovered naturally in the weak-coupling asymptotic regime. This provides a unified description in which deviations from perturbative stopping can be quantified and the onset of perturbative breakdown can be identified. The framework is validated against time-resolved proton energy-loss measurements in a hydrogen discharge plasma and against FCDF benchmarks in the classical and strongly degenerate limits. For partially ionized warm dense carbon, the calculated stopping power remains close to TD-KS-DFT and TD-OF-DFT reference data, while conventional phenomenological and average-atom models tend to overestimate the Bragg-peak region. These results indicate that higher-order phase-shift corrections are essential in the strongly coupled regime and that the present framework provides a consistent non-perturbative description of ion energy loss in partially ionized warm dense plasmas.</jats:p>

title: Temperature-dependent boron-vacancy interaction from aggregation to dissociation in molybdenum and tungsten: Bridging zero-K DFT to finite-temperature thermodynamics/statistical physics
abstract: Bridging zero-K DFT calculations to finite-temperature thermodynamics/statistical-mechanics, we revealed a temperature-dependent mechanism for boron-vacancy interaction from aggregation to dissociation, by examining the concentrations of B-induced point-defects and dissociation energy of B from B n V clusters in Mo and W. Increasing temperature generating thermal vacancies and activating interstitial B migration that promotes the aggregation of B atoms at vacancies to form B n V clusters, which are stable within the temperature ranges of 400–1200 and 600–1400 K in Mo and W, respectively. Exceeding 1200/1400 K in Mo/W, the B n V clusters become unstable and B atoms acquire sufficient energy to dissociate from them. The B dissociation activation energies range from 3.10/3.70 to 3.90/4.50 eV in Mo/W, and the B dissociation from B 1 V, B 2 V, B 3 V, and B 4 V clusters in Mo/W can occur at 1420/1638, 1482/1735, 1307/1576, and 1241/1474 K, respectively. Thus, the dissociation temperature ranges are 1200–1500 and 1400–1800 K in Mo and W, respectively. When the temperature further exceeds the maximum dissociation temperature of 1500/1800 K in Mo/W, B atoms in both B n V clusters and interstitial positions are in a dynamic equilibrium states, i.e., B atoms dissociate from B n V clusters at any time to form vacancies and interstitial B atoms, and conversely interstitial B atoms can also be recaptured by vacancies at any time to reform B n V clusters. In this sense, above 1500/1800 K in Mo/W, B n V clusters, vacancies, and interstitial B atoms should be viewed as transient rather than permanently existing species.

title: Turbomachinery Sizing and Economic Evaluation of Open-Air Brayton Cycle for High-Temperature Small Modular Reactor Applications
abstract: In this study, the applicability of an open-air Brayton cycle (OABC) secondary system coupled with high-temperature reactor heat sources was evaluated in terms of its cycle performance, turbomachinery sizing, and economic viability. Reactor-specific core outlet temperatures were used to determine the OABC turbine inlet temperatures after accounting for a minimum temperature difference of 5 °C across the intermediate heat exchanger (IHX), while a 1% air-side pressure loss across the IHX was also considered. Pressure-ratio optimisation was performed to determine the thermal efficiency, net specific work, and required mass flow rate. The equivalent characteristic diameters of the compressor and turbine were estimated using Smith chart-based preliminary sizing, while the corresponding thermodynamic conditions were used to evaluate the specific capital expenditure (CAPEX) and levelised cost of electricity (LCOE). The results revealed that increasing the turbine inlet temperature improved the optimised system efficiency and net specific work while reducing the mass flow rate required to produce the same electric power output. Accordingly, low-temperature cases such as BWRX-300 and ENTRA1 required substantially larger equivalent characteristic diameters at a given electrical output, whereas the higher-temperature AFR-100, IMSR, and Xe-100 cases exhibited smaller turbomachinery flow-area requirements owing to their lower required air mass flow rates. The economic assessment indicated that increasing both electric power and turbine inlet temperature reduced the specific CAPEX and LCOE of the OABC secondary system. After explicitly including the reactor–cycle IHX in the economic boundary, the specific CAPEX of all reactor cases remained above the AP-1000 and MIGHTR-4 secondary-system-equivalent reference values throughout the investigated 100–600 MWe range. The calculated LCOE for all cases also exceeded the reference LCOE for the AP-1000 NOAK and MIGHTR-4 NOAK cases. These results indicate that higher-temperature reactor conditions substantially reduce the OABC secondary-system cost, although the calculated specific CAPEX and LCOE remain above the adopted reference values under the present assumptions.

title: Advancing a Just and Equitable Climate Transition: Modeling Nuclear Energy and COP30-Driven Sustainable Development
abstract: The COP30 agreement, as illustrated in the provided modeling, represents a critical shift toward a just and equitable transition, ensuring that climate action safeguards vulnerable populations while fostering sustainable development. This study analyzes the significance of nuclear energy in the systemic transition from a carbon-intensive system to a low-carbon future by evaluating energy development scenarios through logical weighting and stochastic modeling. By assigning variables such as Capital Expenditure and temporal weights to COP28, COP29, and COP30, the research quantifies how past international commitments influence future energy trajectories. The findings, derived from the comparative analysis of Scenarios 1, 2, and 3, highlight the urgent need for accelerated emissions reductions and expanded renewable energy deployment. At COP30, the scenarios show relatively similar values, as they follow the trends observed at COP28 and COP29. The fact that Scenario 3 exhibits the highest standard deviation indicates significant volatility in the production of industrial power, hydrogen, and heat using nuclear power plants. The modeling demonstrates that while past events provide a cumulative foundation, the specific weighting of COP30 variables including the Power Generation trends is essential for achieving long-term environmental resilience and green employment. Ultimately, this focuses on the necessity of aligning global development pathways with high-fidelity climate objectives to mitigate long-term risks.

title: Transfer Learning–Based Improvement of Low-Temperature Thermal Conductivity Prediction for N-Hydrogen and ANN-Based Thermophysical Property Modeling of Helium
abstract: The thermophysical properties of cryogenic gases, such as hydrogen, helium, and other low-temperature gases, play a crucial role in nuclear energy applications, particularly in reactor design, superconducting magnet cooling, cryogenic distribution systems, safety assessments, and thermal efficiency. The accurate estimation of these properties over a wide range of operating conditions is essential for reliable cryogenic process design and transient system analysis.Traditionally, thermophysical properties have been predicted using empirical correlations, theoretical equations of state, and experimentally derived formulations, which are implemented in established property packages such as RefProp®, CoolProp®, HEPAK®, and GASPAK®. While these approaches have proven highly effective, deviations may still arise in specific operating regions, particularly at cryogenic temperatures where experimental data are sparse and fluid behavior becomes highly nonlinear.In recent years, deep learning and artificial neural networks (ANNs) have emerged as powerful data-driven tools for modeling complex nonlinear relationships across scientific and engineering applications, including thermophysical property prediction. Rather than replacing established cryogenic property routines, ANN-based approaches may offer a complementary framework for incorporating newly available experimental data sets and refining predictions in operating regions where deviations from reference data are observed.The present work explores the possibility of utilizing the capabilities of ANNs and transfer learning techniques for cryogenic thermophysical property prediction. Residual transfer learning is applied to improve the thermal conductivity prediction for n-hydrogen (normal hydrogen) in the temperature range of 15 to 30 K using published experimental data sets. Helium properties are modeled as a proof-of-concept study to evaluate the capability of the ANN architecture to reproduce the global thermodynamic trends and overall nonlinear variations in cryogenic thermophysical properties, while also examining its limitations in regions with strong local property variations.Furthermore, In addition, a graphical user interface–based module, CRYOProp, has been developed to improve usability and accessibility. The present work highlights the applicability, limitations, and potential of the proposed methodology.

title: Study on Temperature Distribution Characteristics Downstream of Internal Leaking Steam Valves in Power Plants and CFD Simulation
abstract: Internal leakage in power plant valves is often concealed by piping and equipment casings, making it difficult to detect. Yet even small leaks can cause substantial energy losses, especially for steam valves. Current monitoring methods, mainly acoustic and temperature-based, are largely limited to qualitative detection. To address the issues of difficult detection and effective quantitative monitoring of internal leakage in power plant steam valves, a high-temperature and high-pressure test bench was built, and a corresponding numerical model was established to investigate the temperature field distribution downstream of the leaking valve. Experimental and numerical results demonstrate that temperature monitoring is highly sensitive to steam leakage. When leakage occurs, the positive Joule–Thomson effect causes the pipe wall temperature to drop sharply from the valve upstream to its outlet; the temperature then rises rapidly before declining further downstream, with the steady-state peak consistently occurring at 2.5–7.5 DN downstream. Valve leakage causes obvious temperature stratification and severe pressure drop. This process approximates isenthalpic throttling and involves steam phase change. The large pressure differential across the valve also generates high flow velocity and choked flow. In addition, steam pressure and moisture exert a notable influence on temperature distribution. The findings of this study provide a theoretical foundation for quantitative research on valve leakage.

title: Retained fuel removal from plasma-facing materials: effects of baking methods and hydrogen isotope exchange
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tungsten (W) is a prominent plasma-facing material for deuterium-tritium (D-T) fusion reactors, yet T fuel retention in W poses critical challenges to safety and operational viability. This study systematically compares three baking methods—vacuum baking, H2 gas atmosphere baking, and hydrogen (H) plasma baking—for removing D retained in W at 513 K, simulating realistic conditions for T removal in reactors. Experimental results demonstrate that D removal efficiencies reach 75% for vacuum baking after 16 h, 83% for H2 atmosphere baking after 16 h, and 99% for H plasma baking after 1 h. The superior performance of H2 atmosphere and H plasma baking is primarily driven by hydrogen isotope (HI) exchange, with efficiency strongly dependent on the concentration of H introduced into W. Higher H concentrations promote more complete exchange, leading to significantly reduced D retention. A multi-isotope Fill Level model was developed to simulate the end-to-end H plasma exchange process. The simulation reproduces the experimentally observed D removal kinetics and the emergence of HD desorption, with the D retention in good agreement with measurements. The pronounced disparity between H2 atmosphere baking and H plasma baking is fundamentally governed by the quantity of H entering W: H plasma promotes significantly greater H ingress, thereby enhancing HI exchange and resulting in a drastic reduction in D retention. This work provides both experimental validation and modelling support for HI exchange as an efficient T removal strategy.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>A new gyrokinetic code, TEK, was benchmarked in simulating energetic particle (EP)&#xD;driven toroidal Alfven eigenmodes (TAEs) in the simple tokamak configuration chosen&#xD;by the ITPA-EP group for code benchmarking purposes. Linear benchmark has been&#xD;well established by other codes, whereas nonlinear benchmark for this case is lacking.&#xD;This paper presents, besides the linear benchmark, nonlinear results for both single-n&#xD;and multiple-n simulations (n is the toroidal mode number). The nonlinear results&#xD;are in good agreement with an analytical theory on zonal field beat-driven by Alfven&#xD;eigenmodes, partially verifying the correctness of the nonlinear simulations. The&#xD;electromagnetic cancellation problem is mitigated by using the mixed-variable pull-&#xD;back method. title: Impact of ICRH-driven beta-induced Alfvén eigenmode on fast-ion redistribution and ion heating in EAST plasmas
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In magnetically confined plasmas, energetic-particle (EP)-driven instabilities can induce redistribution and losses of energetic ions, thereby affecting plasma heating and confinement. In this work, fast-ion-driven beta-induced Alfvén eigenmode (BAE) excited by ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) was investigated in low-density EAST plasmas using experimentally reconstructed equilibria and profiles. Experimentally, strong ICRH led to a significant increase in ion temperature and plasma stored energy, accompanied by the excitation of an Alfvén eigenmode at 64kHz under 1.6 MW heating power, while no such mode was observed at reduced power. Continuum analysis identified this mode as a core-localized BAE. To interpret these observations, integrated simulations combining TORIC, ASCOT, and GTC were performed. A modified fast-ion distribution function was implemented to capture the strong velocity-space anisotropy of ICRH-generated fast ions. Linear gyrokinetic simulations reproduced the observed BAE frequency and identified a threshold in fast-ion pressure for mode excitation. Orbit-following simulations with realistic wall geometry demonstrated that the BAE induces significant phase-space redistribution and enhances the loss of high-energy fast ions (energy >600keV). Separately, the ASCOT power-deposition analysis shows that the strong BAE reduces the collisional power transferred from fast ions to thermal ions, thereby suppressing the fast-ion contribution to ion heating and limiting the increase in ion temperature. As the measured BAE activity decreases in Phase B, recovery of this ion-heating channel explains the subsequent rise in ion temperature. These results clarify the interplay between ICRH-generated fast ions, BAE activity, and ion heating, and provide insights into optimizing fast-ion confinement and heating efficiency in future burning plasma devices.</jats:p>

title: Damping and accumulation characteristics of flow driven by fishbone instability
abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The persistence of fishbone-driven flows across successive bursts is critical to their potential role in regulating turbulence and improving core confinement, yet the damping characteristics of such flows have not been experimentally characterized. Here we report the first direct measurement of the damping rate of fishbone-driven flows using Doppler reflectometry on the EAST tokamak. The experimentally obtained damping rate exceeds prior theoretical predictions, and this discrepancy can be reconciled by incorporating the effective charge number $Z_{\text{eff}}$ into the accalculation of the damping rate. Furthermore, we observe that flow accumulation occurs when the time interval between successive fishbone bursts is sufficiently short, and we estimate the critical inter-burst interval threshold for accumulation to be approximately 1 ms under the present discharge conditions. These results establish an essential experimental foundation for understanding the temporal persistence of fishbone-driven flows and their implications for transport barrier dynamics.</jats:p>

title: Specimen-Level Evaluation of Machine-Learning-Based Eddy-Current Testing for Chromium Coating Thickness Estimation in Accident-Tolerant Fuel Cladding
abstract: Maintaining a uniform chromium (Cr) coating thickness on zirconium-alloy cladding is critical to nuclear-fuel accident tolerance. Eddy current testing (ECT) with machine learning (ML) is a promising non-destructive method, but existing studies often use random train–test splits that leak specimen identity, overestimating accuracy on unseen rods, and rarely quantify the measurement noise floor. We propose a specimen-level evaluation framework, leave-one-specimen-out (LOSO) cross-validation with nested hyperparameter tuning, for ML-based ECT thickness estimation. Applied to a six-frequency (3.5–6 MHz) dataset of ten Cr-coated specimens (3.9–20.1 ), it exposes substantial over-optimism: a greedy frequency-selection scheme scoring 0.196 RMSE in-sample degrades to 0.506 under leakage-free evaluation. A mixed-effects variance decomposition establishes a single-channel measurement repeatability floor of 0.10 as a conservative lower bound for achievable RMSE and prediction intervals. A uniform multi-frequency Gaussian process regression improves RMSE from 0.265 to 0.205 and halves prediction-interval miscalibration, a consistent trend whose 95% bootstrap confidence interval still includes zero at ten specimens ( P (better) = 0.84). Learning frequency or component relevance overfits on small datasets, confirming uniform fusion as the robust choice. This work establishes a leakage-free evaluation standard and a repeatability-based performance reference for ECT thickness estimation.

title: Estimating Porosity and Permeability in the Uranium-bearing Stratum Based on LSTM and Transfer Learning Under Limited Supportive Data
abstract: Porosity and permeability are among the key factors influencing the effectiveness of in-situ leaching of uranium. Common methods for obtaining porosity and permeability of cores can generally be classified into two categories: direct measurement and indirect estimation. Traditional indirect estimation relying on well-logging data often requires huge manpower and time. To address this issue, this study introduced machine learning with the aim of deeply exploring the intrinsic relationships between well-logging data and porosity and permeability of cores to achieve rapid and intelligent identification of porosity and permeability. Considering the limited amount of measured porosity and permeability of cores in the study area, an algorithm combining Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks with transfer learning was constructed and optimized to effectively identify the porosity and permeability of the target area. The test results show that the algorithm model achieves relative prediction errors of approximately 14% for porosity and 11% for permeability. This study provides a feasible reference for predicting porosity and permeability in sandstone-type uranium deposits where measured core data are difficult to obtain, and it also has the potential to be applied to other resource mining areas with limited measured porosity and permeability data.

title: Thermomechanical low cycle fatigue assessment of the W-armoured ITER First Wall Panel
abstract: The recent transition of the ITER actively cooled First Wall Panel (FWP) from beryllium to tungsten (W) armour tiles necessitates the requalification of the component under high heat flux (HHF) testing. A soft copper (Cu) interlayer is utilized to accommodate the significant thermal expansion mismatch between the W tiles and the underlying CuCrZr heat sink. This study investigates the low cycle fatigue (LCF) performance of the Cu compliance layer using a thermomechanical elastoplastic finite element simulation in Ansys APDL. The simulation models a single tile unit cell subjected to 2 MW/m 2 HHF cycling, utilizing Chaboche non-linear kinematic hardening to accurately capture strain hardening within the Cu and CuCrZr layers. Results indicate that the simulated fatigue degradation can produce effective surface-level debonding of the W/Cu joint before the required 30,000 HHF cycles. The LCF life of the Cu interlayer is predominantly limited by the 12 mm W tile thickness and the minimum water coolant temperature of 70 °C. Furthermore, a novel cycle jump simulation demonstrates that fatigue fronts develop near debonded corners after approximately 8000 cycles, significantly accelerating subsequent interfacial failure. Conversely, substituting the Cu interlayer with a W-to-CuCrZr functionally graded material (FGM) eliminated cyclic plastic yielding, presenting a highly effective design alternative for future high heat flux components. Despite not substituting a design-by-experiment approach, these findings provide a quantitative basis for understanding thermomechanical degradation in the ITER flat tile geometry and highlight critical parameters for upcoming experimental validation.

title: Future-Ready Nuclear Engineering Education: Integrating AI, Digital Systems, and Advanced Technologies to Close Critical Skills Gaps
abstract: The U.S. nuclear sector faces a workforce challenge of national scale. U.S. Department of Energy projections indicate the nuclear workforce may need to grow from roughly 100 000 to approximately 375 000 workers by 2050 to support construction, operations, and supply chain roles across advanced reactor deployment. Meeting this demand requires not only more graduates but also graduates prepared for a qualitatively different operating environment. Modern nuclear facilities function as closed-loop, data-driven, cyber-physical systems in which digital instrumentation and control, artificial intelligence–assisted monitoring, digital twin modeling, and cybersecurity governance are now routine features of plant operation. This paper proposes a general, four-layer curriculum framework (physical systems, measurement and control, digital intelligence, and security and governance) intended to help any ABET-accredited nuclear engineering or nuclear engineering technology program map these competencies onto existing degree structures without necessarily increasing credit hour requirements. The framework preserves the traditional physics-based and fundamentals-based core of nuclear engineering education while adding explicit, regulatory-anchored coverage of digital and cyber-physical competencies as a complement to that core rather than a replacement for it. To illustrate how the framework can be instantiated in practice, the paper presents a single-institution case study: the Thomas Edison State University PSEG-Supported Nuclear Workforce Development Initiative, comprising six stackable undergraduate certificates and three newly developed courses, mapped to ABET Engineering Technology Accreditation Commission and Engineering Accreditation Commission outcomes using a three-level Introduced/Reinforced/Mastered framework. The case study is offered as one worked example of the general framework, not as its primary contribution, and the paper explicitly discusses applicability beyond commercial nuclear power, including fuel cycle, defense, and national laboratory pathways, and the risk that expanded digital systems content could crowd out fundamentals if not deliberately guarded against. The paper’s contributions are (1) a general, system-aligned curriculum architecture usable by any nuclear program; (2) a documented single-institution implementation case study with governance timeline and enrollment projections, offered for adaptation rather than replication in kind; and (3) explicit regulatory anchoring intended to make each curriculum element independently verifiable and transferable.

title: Flow-Induced Vibration Characteristics of M310 and Novel Segmented Fuel Rods under Single-Spacer-Grid-Failure Conditions
abstract: A reduced-order Euler–Bernoulli beam model with four degrees of freedom per node is used to compare the flow-induced vibration responses of a conventional M310 fuel rod and a novel segmented-design fuel rod (NSDFR) under intact and complete single-spacer-grid-loss conditions. The numerical implementation is verified against published simply supported and elastically supported beam benchmarks; the largest difference in the first natural frequency is 3.57%. Model adequacy for the intended global-bending analysis is further assessed by effective modal mass, direct modal-truncation convergence, and axial-resolution sensitivity. Across the 18 structural states, the first 20 modes account for 0.872 to 0.920 of the lateral effective mass. Relative to the 20-mode solution, the maximum difference in spatial root-mean-square (RMS) response is 0.325% with 8 modes, 0.098% with 12 modes, and 0.004% with 16 modes. The flow excitation is prescribed using the experimentally informed transverse-velocity profile and semi-empirical response relations reported in the literature. For the intact state, the predicted total peak responses are 0.0601 mm for M310 and 0.0450 mm for NSDFR. Complete loss of the bottom grid produces the largest linear response indicator for both rods, whereas top-grid loss is markedly more severe for NSDFR than for M310. A damping sensitivity study changes response magnitude but not the ranking of critical cases. The model is intended for comparative screening of global bending and support-loss location.

title: Molecular dynamics modeling of Zr-alloying effects on cascade-induced defect evolution in U-Zr metallic fuels
abstract: Cascade-induced defect evolution in U-Zr alloys plays a critical role in determining the irradiation resistance and microstructural stability of metallic nuclear fuels. In this study, molecular dynamics simulations are employed to investigate cascade collision processes and defect evolution behavior in the pure α-U, pure γ-U, δ-(U, Zr), and γ-(U, Zr) phases under different PKA energies and temperatures. The results show that the δ-(U, Zr) phase exhibits a significantly higher peak Frenkel pair population than the pure α-U phase at lower temperatures, whereas the γ-(U, Zr) phase shows reduced peak defect production compared with the pure γ-U phase at elevated temperatures. This phase-dependent behavior is primarily attributed to the reduction in TDEs induced by Zr alloying, which alteres the probability of atomic displacement during the ballistic stage of cascade evolution. Moreover, the δ-(U, Zr) phase forms more numerous and smaller defect clusters than the pure α-U phase, owing to its higher defect diffusivities and weaker same-type defect binding tendencies. In contrast, high defect diffusivities and negative defect binding energies in the γ-U and γ-(U, Zr) phases promote vacancy-interstitial recombination and lead to predominantly isolated surviving defects. These results reveal the effects of Zr alloying on cascade-induced defect evolution in U-Zr systems and provide insights into the irradiation resistance of metallic nuclear fuels.

title: Deuterium retention in tungsten after deuterium–nitrogen co-bombardment
abstract: In order to reduce the edge plasma temperature in fusion reactor divertors such as ITER’s, the introduction of radiating elements (i.e., impurity gas seeding) may be necessary. Nitrogen has been proposed for that purpose due to its good radiation characteristics in the edge plasma temperature range; however, it has the added complication that it will interact chemically with both the hydrogenic fuel and any metal surfaces. The current study looks at the influence of nitrogen co-bombardment on deuterium retention in tungsten by comparing deuterium only and combined deuterium-nitrogen implantation in tungsten with 1% to 10% N at 300–700 K and with energies of 500 eV/D + and 1000 eV/N + . After implantation, thermal desorption spectroscopy (TDS) is used to measure the amount of deuterium retained, and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) is used to investigate nitride formation on the surface. We observe an order-of-magnitude increase in deuterium retention in the temperature range ∼ 500–600 K. This increase occurs for N + /D + ratios as low as 1% and is accompanied by large-scale blistering of the surface. XPS analysis of the co-bombarded surfaces indicate the formation of a tungsten-nitride layer from room temperature to 700 K. We believe that a change in the nature of the tungsten-nitride layer around 500 K creates a permeation barrier affecting the ability of deuterium to diffuse to the surface and increasing deuterium retention.

title: Experimental and Numerical Investigation of Shear Capacity for Concrete Walls with High Reinforcement Ratio Considering Internal Voids
abstract: ABSTRACT The high density of reinforcement in nuclear containment structures often leads to unintentional internal voids due to construction difficulties. This study evaluates the cyclic performance of reinforced concrete shear walls with high reinforcement ratios and low aspect ratios, specifically addressing these construction-induced defects. Through a comprehensive experimental and numerical program, six specimens were tested under cyclic loading, with artificial voids introduced as primary variables. Results indicate that global responses remain similar, however voids significantly accelerate post-peak strength degradation and localize damage by disrupting internal shear transfer mechanisms. The developed finite element model, validated within a 5% error margin, was utilized for an extensive parametric study. The analysis identifies the void area ratio as the governing factor, showing a linear strength reduction that becomes more pronounced beyond a 20% ratio. Based on these findings, a practical evaluation-oriented approach is proposed to quantify shear strength reduction as a function of the void area ratio. This research provides essential guidance for the structural assessment and maintenance of heavily reinforced nuclear facilities containing internal defects.

title: Development of a Low Density Calibration Source Prepared with Polyurethane Foam for HPGe Detector Gamma-Ray Spectrometry
abstract: Stable, low-density reference materials are important for gamma-ray spectrometric measurements of low-density materials, particularly when conventional solid matrices or gaseous standards are unavailable or impractical. In this study, a low-density solid reference material was prepared by incorporating 0.2 g of BL-5, a Canadian Certified Reference Material for uranium ore, into a two-component, rapid-curing rigid polyurethane (PU) foam matrix. Three nominally identical samples were prepared to evaluate reproducibility. The cured PU foam had a density of approximately 0.130 g·cm -3 . Gamma-ray measurements were performed using a 78.5 % relative-efficiency n-type HPGe detector. Full-energy peak efficiencies were determined using a CBSS-2 volumetric multi-gamma reference source and transferred to the PU foam-BL-5 matrix by correcting for differences in photon attenuation. Self-attenuation corrections were calculated using NIST XCOM data, while true coincidence summing corrections were obtained with EFFTRAN. The experimental configuration was independently validated using RayXpert Monte Carlo simulations. The mean measured activities of 238 U, 210 Pb, and 226 Ra were 170± 10, 181 ± 6, and 174 ± 5 Bq, respectively, demonstrating excellent preparation reproducibility. These results indicate that rigid PU foam is a promising stable, substantially lower-density matrix for gamma-ray spectrometric reference materials.
